speaker: Patrick Collison
question: In developer-facing financial infrastructure, why does shipping a major new version of a core API take years once a platform reaches scale?
guest: Back in 2022, we realized that a couple of the core abstractions in Stripe were just not the right long-term abstractions, and we had to fix that, so we designed a bunch of V2 APIs. Historically we had drawn distinctions and represented separately things like end customers, accounts, and recipients for different kinds of payments, and we're unifying all of those into the same entity representation. It's been a long journey, and the reason is that it's not that useful to just define these APIs in isolation. If we just wanted to define them in isolation, that's a pretty easy thing to do. The thing that's difficult is making them interoperable with all the existing things at Stripe and building translation layers. And then figuring out with our customers what a sensible upgrade path looks like, because we control our codebase, we don't control theirs. In certain respects it feels like an instruction set migration for a chip architecture, where the instruction set itself is easy, but all the coexistence questions become hard.

points.core: Designing the new API abstractions in isolation is relatively easy.
points.note: Accept: specifying clean v2 schemas or unified entity models on a blank slate is straightforward compared to migration. Do not credit: claiming API design itself is the primary multi-year bottleneck.

points.core: Building internal translation layers for legacy interoperability dominates the engineering effort.
points.note: Accept: coexistence complexity, bidirectional adapters, or translation layers keeping new APIs interoperable with existing internal systems and v1 objects. Do not credit: vague mentions of 'backward compatibility' without identifying internal coexistence/translation work.

points.core: Platform providers cannot force migrations because customers control their own codebases.
points.note: Accept: asymmetric control over client integrations requiring gradual, non-breaking upgrade paths (analogous to hardware instruction-set coexistence). Do not credit: generic advice to 'write good migration docs' or 'communicate deprecations early.'

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because at scale the API stops being a product you can redesign and becomes a contract that thousands of businesses have built money-moving systems on top of. Three things compound.

First, backward compatibility is nearly absolute. Integrations sit inside checkout flows, ledgers, and reconciliation jobs that customers rarely touch, so breaking changes mean lost revenue or misrouted funds for them. Platforms like Stripe therefore pin each account to a version and maintain translation layers indefinitely, and any new version must coexist with every old one.

Second, the abstractions themselves are hard to get right. A core payments API must model cards, bank debits, wallets, asynchronous confirmations, authentication steps like 3D Secure, disputes, and refunds across many countries and regulatory regimes. A flawed abstraction is costly to undo, so design takes long iteration with real users. Stripe's PaymentIntents took roughly two years to design and launch, and its API v2 followed a similarly multi-year path.

Third, the migration is the real project: SDKs, documentation, dashboards, webhooks, partner plugins, and internal systems all need updating, and users only move when the benefit clearly outweighs their re-integration cost and risk.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Once a financial infrastructure platform reaches scale, a core API is no longer just an interface, but a live contract governing money movement across thousands of businesses. Because merchants avoid rewriting working payment flows and cannot tolerate downtime, platforms cannot force abrupt breaking changes. Instead, engineers must build bidirectional translation layers so old and new versions operate seamlessly over the same ledgers, webhooks, and reconciliation pipelines. At scale, every undocumented quirk, timing behavior, and error code becomes load-bearing for customers' checkout and accounting systems.

Meanwhile, a new core abstraction must unify fragmented card networks, legacy banking rails, and regional mandates like Strong Customer Authentication while matching years of accumulated edge-case parity. Proving correctness requires prolonged shadow-traffic testing, idempotency verification, and regulatory sign-off, since subtle state-machine bugs risk double charges or settlement drift. Finally, shipping spans an entire ecosystem: SDKs, third-party plugins, and risk-averse enterprises tied to rigid compliance and release cycles must validate the design in production before a new API truly becomes the platform standard.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Once a payments platform is big, a new API version is a migration problem more than a coding problem. Thousands of businesses have built checkout flows, accounting, reconciliation and compliance processes on the old API's exact behavior, including its quirks. Money is involved, so a subtle change can cause double charges, missed payouts or broken audit trails. Developers expect integrations to work for years without changes. Stripe, for example, pins each account to a dated API version and keeps old versions running through compatibility layers, because forced upgrades would break revenue-critical code that merchants may not even have engineers maintaining anymore.

A redesign also has to cover everything that has built up around the API: payment methods, regional regulations like SCA, webhooks, SDKs in many languages, docs, dashboards and partner plugins. Stripe's move from Charges to PaymentIntents took years of parallel support. Its "v2" APIs have rolled out gradually, one area at a time. Teams have to run both models side by side, offer migration tools, and wait for a long tail of users to move. That backward-compatibility burden, not the new design, is what stretches the timeline into years.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Once a developer-facing financial platform reaches scale, a core API becomes an effectively permanent contract embedded in millions of live, revenue-critical integrations. Unlike consumer software, financial infrastructure cannot force breaking upgrades without risking halted payments, broken reconciliation, or corrupted ledgers. Shipping a major new version therefore requires running old and new models side by side—often through complex compatibility and translation layers—while preserving strict accounting invariants, idempotency, and audit trails across both.

Beyond the endpoints themselves, a core API anchors a vast ecosystem: strongly typed SDKs across many languages, webhook and event schemas, dashboards, reporting pipelines, sandboxes, and third-party partner integrations must all evolve coherently. Every change also intersects with regulatory, banking-network, and compliance requirements that vary by jurisdiction and cannot be bypassed for speed.

Finally, because design mistakes in a major version will be supported for a decade or more, teams invest heavily in upfront modeling, private betas, and incremental migrations with real customers before committing to a public release.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
At scale, a core financial API is a contract that thousands of businesses build their own systems around. A change to how a payment is retried or when a webhook fires can lead to duplicate charges, missed refunds, or reconciliation errors. Some of those dependencies are buried in customer code the platform can’t see.

The platform has to design the new behavior, prove it works across existing accounts and edge cases, and give customers a way to migrate on their own schedules. That often means running both versions in production, updating SDKs and documentation, rolling out in stages, and keeping a way to roll back. Customers may need to change their own billing and accounting systems before they can switch. Writing the new API is one part of the job. Making it safe for businesses to adopt while money keeps moving is what takes years.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
At scale, a core financial API is a contract with thousands of businesses, each with its own release schedule. Even a small change in what a payment status means can cause a merchant to ship an order too early or record the wrong amount. The platform can release new code in a day, but it can’t upgrade every customer’s integration that day.

That makes compatibility and migration a large part of the work. Old and new versions may need to agree on the same transaction for months, including when a payment made under one version is refunded or disputed under the other. The platform has to test those cases, update SDKs and documentation, and give customers time to verify that their books still reconcile. Much of the calendar time goes into making the transition safe while money keeps moving.
